content: Lily of the Valley, scientifically known as Convallaria majalis, is the sole species within the genus Convallaria, which belongs to the flowering plant family Ruscaceae. Historically, it was classified under the lily family (Liliaceae) or its own family, Convallariaceae. This woodland plant is native to the cool temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere, including Asia, Europe, and a limited native population in the eastern United States (Convallaria majalis var. montana). It is a herbaceous perennial plant that propagates extensively through underground stems called rhizomes, which produce stolons. These stolons give rise to numerous stems each spring. The stems typically grow to a height of 15–30 cm and bear one or two leaves measuring 10–25 cm in length. Flowering stems have two leaves and a raceme of 5–15 flowers at the apex. The flowers are white (occasionally pink), bell-shaped, and measure 5–10 mm in diameter. They are sweetly fragrant and bloom in late spring, or as early as March in regions with mild winters. The fruit is a small orange-red berry, 5–7 mm in diameter, containing a few large seeds that are whitish to brownish in color. These seeds dry into translucent, round beads measuring 1–3 mm in width. The plant is self-sterile, meaning colonies of a single clone do not produce seeds. There are three recognized subspecies, which some botanists have occasionally classified as distinct species: Convallaria majalis var. keiskei: Found in China and Japan, characterized by red fruit and bowl-shaped flowers. Convallaria majalis var. majalis: Native to Eurasia, distinguished by white midribs on the flowers. Convallaria majalis var. montana: Found in the United States, with green-tinted midribs on the flowers. Garden Use Convallaria majalis is a popular garden plant, cultivated for its fragrant flowers. Various forms are grown, including those with double flowers, rose-colored flowers, variegated foliage, and larger-sized plants. However, it is sometimes considered a weed due to its ability to spread aggressively across gardens and other areas, making it difficult to control or remove. Additionally, the plant serves as a food source for the larvae of certain Lepidoptera species, such as the Grey Chi moth. Herbalism The leaves and flowers of Lily of the Valley contain cardiac glycosides, including convallatoxin, which have been used medicinally for centuries. However, in excessive doses, these compounds can be toxic. Pets and children are particularly at risk if they ingest the plant. It also contains convallamarin, which has effects similar to digitalis. In medieval times, herbalists used it as a substitute for foxglove. During the First World War, it was employed to treat victims of mustard gas exposure. Due to its potent effects, Lily of the Valley should only be used under the supervision of a qualified herbalist. Legend and Tradition The flower is also known as Our Lady's Tears in Christian legend, as it is said to have sprung from the tears Mary shed at the foot of the cross. Another legend claims that the flowers emerged from the blood of St. George during his battle with the dragon. Other names for the plant include May Lily, May Bells, Lily Constancy, Ladder-to-Heaven, Male Lily, and Muguet. Traditionally, Lily of the Valley is sold on the streets of France on May 1st. It was declared the national flower of Finland in 1982. The Norwegian municipality of Lunner features a Lily of the Valley in its coat of arms. It is also the official flower of several fraternities and sororities, including Alpha Delta Phi, Pi Kappa Alpha, Kappa Sigma, Delta Omicron, Alpha Epsilon Phi, and Alpha Phi. The name Lily of the Valley is used in some English translations of the Bible in Song of Songs 2:1, though it is uncertain whether the Hebrew word shoshana originally referred to this species. The symbolic meaning of the flower is You will find happiness.
